slides.text:
A loop repeats a block of code. Go has a single loop keyword, `for`, and it takes several shapes: a counter, a condition, nothing at all, or a walk over a value.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
repeat while the condition holds
    do this
    maybe skip to the next lap
    maybe stop the loop early

slides.text:
Two sessions:

- **Session 1:** the counter, the condition, the loop with no end and `break`
- **Session 2:** `range`, `continue` and loops inside loops

The classic `for` has three parts. The first runs once before the loop, the second is checked before every lap, and the third runs after every lap.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
Keep only the condition and the loop runs while it is true. Keep nothing and it runs until a `break` stops it.

exercises.guide: Repeat a block while a counter climbs.

chunks.guide: `for` has three parts: the setup, the condition and the step. The block repeats while the condition is true.
This line runs once, after the loop ends.

exercises.title: Why does it not compile?
exercises.guide: Read the message, then pick the cause.
options: A `for` loop cannot be followed by code
`i` needs a type before the loop
exercises.explanation: A variable declared in the setup of a `for` lives only in the loop. After the closing brace it is gone.

exercises.title: Loop on a condition
exercises.guide: Keep only the condition, and loop while it holds.

chunks.guide: With just a condition, `for` works like a `while` loop. You change the variable yourself inside the block.

notes.text: No setup and no step, only the check.

chunks.guide: The loop ended because the condition became false.

exercises.title: A loop with no end
exercises.guide: Write a loop with no condition and stop it with `break`.

chunks.guide: A `for` with nothing after it repeats forever. `break` leaves the loop at once, and the code after it runs.

notes.text: Jumps out of the nearest loop.

output.text:
tick 1
tick 2
tick 3
out of the loop

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: When `i` is 3 the `break` ends the loop before the print, so only 1 and 2 appear. Then the line after the loop runs.

slides.text:
`range` walks over a value. Over a number it counts from 0 up to one less than that number. Over a string it gives each character with its position.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
for each position and character
    of the text
        use them

slides.text: `continue` skips the rest of the current lap and starts the next one. `break` ends the whole loop, but only the innermost one when loops are nested.

exercises.title: Range over a number
exercises.guide: Repeat a block a fixed number of times with `range`.

chunks.guide: `range 3` gives 0, 1 and 2, one value per lap.
When you do not need the number, leave the variable out.

output.text:
round 0
round 1
round 2
hi
hi
done

exercises.title: Range over a string
exercises.guide: Walk a string one character at a time.

chunks.guide: `range` over a string gives the position and the character, as a `rune`. `string(r)` turns it back into text.
Use `_` for a value you do not need. Go would reject an unused variable.

exercises.title: What kind of error is it?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the kind of error.
exercises.explanation: `i` is declared by the loop and never used. Go refuses that, so write `_` in its place.

chunks.guide: A counter for the skipped laps.
`continue` ends the current lap and jumps to the next one. The print below it runs only for odd numbers.

notes.text: Goes straight to the next lap.

chunks.guide: Show how many laps were skipped.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `break` leaves only the inner loop. The outer loop goes on, so each `i` prints once, with `j` equal to 1.
